entries.b3abd9a83f99f104edcfa52244cd2d07576ba854: <div sID="gen9373" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Job.7" sID="Job.7"/> <div eID="gen9373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9374" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9375" type="x-p"/> Job, in this chapter, goes on to express the bitter sense he had of his calamities and to justify himself in his desire of death. I. He complains to himself and his friends of his troubles, and the constant agitation he was in, <reference osisRef="Job.7.1-Job.7.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. He turns to God, and expostulates with him (<reference osisRef="Job.7.7-Job.7.21">ver. 7</reference>, to the end), in which, 1. He pleads the final period which death puts to our present state, <reference osisRef="Job.7.7-Job.7.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. 2. He passionately complains of the miserable condition he was now in, <reference osisRef="Job.7.11-Job.7.16">ver. 11-16</reference>. 3. He wonders that God will thus contend with him, and begs for the pardon of his sins and a speedy release out of his miseries, <reference osisRef="Job.7.17-Job.7.21">ver. 17-21</reference>. It is hard to methodize the speeches of one who owned himself almost desperate, <reference osisRef="Job.6.26">ch. vi. 26</reference>.
entries.0d953670d2b567068c92fd84bfb80e358950bd81: <div eID="gen9375" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9374" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Reply to Eliphaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9376" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="italic">Is there</hi> not an appointed time to man upon earth? <hi type="italic">are not</hi> his days also like the days of a hireling? <hi type="super">2</hi> As a servant earnestly desireth the shadow, and as an hireling looketh for <hi type="italic">the reward of</hi> his work: <hi type="super">3</hi> So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me. <hi type="super">4</hi> When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day. <hi type="super">5</hi> My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust; my skin is broken, and become loathsome. 6 My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope. <div eID="gen9376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9377" type="x-p"/> Job is here excusing what he could not justify, even his inordinate desire of death. Why should he not wish for the termination of life, which would be the termination of his miseries? To enforce this reason he argues, <div eID="gen9377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9378" type="x-p"/> I. From the general condition of man upon earth (<reference osisRef="Job.7.1">v. 1</reference>): "He <hi type="italic">is of few days, and full of trouble.</hi> Every man must die shortly, and every man has some reason (more or less) to desire to die shortly; and therefore why should you impute it to me as so heinous a crime that I wish to die shortly?" Or thus: "Pray mistake not my desires of death, as if I thought the time appointed of God could be anticipated: no, I know very well that that is fixed; only in such language as this I take the liberty to express my present uneasiness: <hi type="italic">Is there not an appointed time (a warfare,</hi> so the word is) to <hi type="italic">man upon earth?</hi> and <hi type="italic">are not his days</hi> here <hi type="italic">like the days of a hireling?</hi>" Observe, 1. Man's present place. He is upon earth, which God <hi type="italic">has given to the children of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.115.16">Ps. cxv. 16</reference>. This bespeaks man's meanness and inferiority. How much below the inhabitants of yonder elevated and refined regions is he situated! It also bespeaks God's mercy to him. He is yet upon the earth, not under it; on earth, not in hell. Our time on earth is limited and short, according to the narrow bounds of this earth; but heaven cannot be measured, nor the days of heaven numbered. 2. His continuance in that place. Is there not a time appointed for his abode here? Yes, certainly there is, and it is easy to say by whom the appointment is made, even by him that made us and set us here. We are not to be on this earth always, nor long, but for a certain time, which is determined by him in whose hand our times are. We are not to think that we are governed by the blind fortune of the Epicureans, but by the wise, holy, and sovereign counsel of God. 3. His condition during that continuance. Man's life is <hi type="italic">a warfare,</hi> and <hi type="italic">as the days of a hireling.</hi> We are every one of us to look upon ourselves in this world, (1.) As soldiers, exposed to hardship and in the midst of enemies; we must serve and be under command; and, when our warfare is accomplished, we must be disbanded, dismissed with either shame or honour, according to what we have done in the body. (2.) As day-labourers, that have the work of the day to do in its day and must make up their account at night. <div eID="gen9378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9379" type="x-p"/> II. From his own condition at this time. He had as much reason, he thought, to wish for death, as a poor servant or hireling that is tired with his work has to wish for the shadows of the evening, when he shall receive his penny and go to rest, <reference osisRef="Job.7.2">v. 2</reference>. The darkness of the night is as welcome to the labourer as the light of the morning is to the watchman, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.6">Ps. cxxx. 6</reference>. The God of nature has provided for the repose of labourers, and no wonder that they desire it. <hi type="italic">The sleep of the labouring man is sweet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.12">Eccl. v. 12</reference>. No pleasure more grateful, more relishing, to the luxurious than rest to the laborious; nor can any rich man take so much satisfaction in the return of his rent-days as the hireling in his day's wages. The comparison is plain, the application is concise and somewhat obscure, but we must supply a word or two, and then it is easy: exactness of language is not to be expected from one in Job's condition. "<hi type="italic">As a servant earnestly desires the shadow, so</hi> and for the same reason I earnestly desire death; for <hi type="italic">I am made to possess,</hi> &c." Hear his complaint. <div eID="gen9379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9380" type="x-p"/> 1. His days were useless, and had been so a great while. He was wholly taken off from business, and utterly unfit for it. Every day was a burden to him, because he was in no capacity of doing good, or of spending it to any purpose. <hi type="italic">Et vitæ partem non attigit ullam—He could not fill up his time with any thing that would turn to account.</hi> This he calls <hi type="italic">possessing months of vanity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.7.3">v. 3</reference>. It very much increases the affliction of sickness and age, to a good man, that he is thereby forced from his usefulness. He insists not so much upon it that they are days in which he has no pleasure as that they are days in which he does not good; on that account they are months of vanity. But when we are disabled to work for God, if we will but sit still quietly for him, it is all one; we shall be accepted. <div eID="gen9380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9381" type="x-p"/> 2. His nights were restless, <reference osisRef="Job.7.3-Job.7.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. The night relieves the toil and fatigue of the day, not only to the labourers, but to the sufferers: if a sick man can but get a little sleep in the night, it helps nature, and it is hoped that he will do well, <reference osisRef="John.11.12">John xi. 12</reference>. However, be the trouble what it will, sleep gives some intermission to the cares, and pains, and griefs, that afflict us; it is the parenthesis of our sorrows. But poor Job could not gain this relief. (1.) His nights were wearisome, and, instead of taking any rest, he did but tire himself more with tossing to and fro until morning. Those that are in great uneasiness, through pain of body or anguish of mind, think by changing sides, changing places, changing postures, to get some ease; but, while the cause is the same within, it is all to no purpose; it is but a resemblance of a fretful discontented spirit, that is ever shifting, but never easy. This made him dread the night as much as the servant desires it, and, when he lay down, to say, <hi type="italic">When will the night be gone?</hi> (2.) These <hi type="italic">wearisome nights</hi> were <hi type="italic">appointed</hi> to him. God, who determines the times before appointed, had allotted him such nights as these. Whatever is at any time grievous to us, it is good to see it appointed for us, that we may acquiesce in the event, not only as unavoidable because appointed, but as therefore designed for some holy end. When we have comfortable nights we must see them also appointed to us and be thankful for them; many better than we have wearisome nights. <div eID="gen9381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9382" type="x-p"/> 3. His body was noisome, <reference osisRef="Job.7.5">v. 5</reference>. His sores bred worms, the scabs were like clods of dust, and his skin was broken; so evil was the disease which cleaved fast to him. See what vile bodies we have, and what little reason we have to pamper them or be proud of them; they have in themselves the principles of their own corruption: as fond as we are of them now, the time may come when we may loathe them and long to get rid of them. <div eID="gen9382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9383" type="x-p"/> 4. His life was hastening apace towards a period, <reference osisRef="Job.7.6">v. 6</reference>. He thought he had no reason to expect a long life, for he found himself declining fast (<reference osisRef="Job.7.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle,</hi> that is, "My time is now but short, and there are but a few sands more in my glass, which will speedily run out." Natural motions are more swift near the centre. Job thought his days ran swiftly because he thought he should soon be at his journey's end; he looked upon them as good as spent already, and he was therefore without hope of being restored to his former prosperity. It is applicable to man's life in general. Our days are like a weaver's shuttle, thrown from one side of the web to the other in the twinkling of an eye, and then back again, to and fro, until at length it is quite exhausted of the thread it carried, and then we <hi type="italic">cut off, like a weaver, our life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.38.12">Isa. xxxviii. 12</reference>. Time hastens on apace; the motion of it cannot be stopped, and, when it is past, it cannot be recalled. While we are living, as we are sowing (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">Gal. vi. 8</reference>), so we are weaving. Every day, like the shuttle, leaves a thread behind it. Many weave the spider's web, which will fail them, <reference osisRef="Job.8.14">ch. viii. 14</reference>. If we are weaving to ourselves holy garments and robes of righteousness, we shall have the benefit of them when our work comes to be reviewed and every man shall reap as he sowed and wear as he wove.
entries.32bf4f869bf1a8960083231db40b69b34c1a462a: <div eID="gen9383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9384" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> O remember that my life <hi type="italic">is</hi> wind: mine eye shall no more see good. <hi type="super">8</hi> The eye of him that hath seen me shall see me no <hi type="italic">more:</hi> thine eyes <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon me, and I <hi type="italic">am</hi> not. <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away: so he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no <hi type="italic">more.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more. <hi type="super">11</hi> Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. 12 <hi type="italic">Am</hi> I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me? 13 When I say, My bed shall comfort me, my couch shall ease my complaint; <hi type="super">14</hi> Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions: <hi type="super">15</hi> So that my soul chooseth strangling, <hi type="italic">and</hi> death rather than my life. <hi type="super">16</hi> I loathe <hi type="italic">it;</hi> I would not live alway: let me alone; for my days <hi type="italic">are</hi> vanity. <div eID="gen9384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9385" type="x-p"/> Job, observing perhaps that his friends, though they would not interrupt him in his discourse, yet began to grow weary, and not to heed much what he said, here turns to God, and speaks to him. If men will not hear us, God will; if men cannot help us, he can; for his arm is not shortened, neither is his ear heavy. Yet we must not go to school to Job here to learn how to speak to God; for, it must be confessed, there is a great mixture of passion and corruption in what he here says. But, if God be not extreme to mark what his people say amiss, let us also make the best of it. Job is here begging of God either to ease him or to end him. He here represents himself to God, <div eID="gen9385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9386" type="x-p"/> I. As a dying man, surely and speedily dying. It is good for us, when we are sick, to think and speak of death, for sickness is sent on purpose to put us in mind of it; and, if we be duly mindful of it ourselves, we may in faith put God in mind of it, as Job does here (<reference osisRef="Job.7.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">O remember that my life is wind.</hi> He recommends himself to God as an object of his pity and compassion, with this consideration, that he was a very weak frail creature, his abode in this world short and uncertain, his removal out of it sure and speedy, and his return to it again impossible and never to be expected—that his life was wind, as the lives of all men are, noisy perhaps and blustering, like the wind, but vain and empty, soon gone, and, when gone, past recall. God had compassion on Israel, <hi type="italic">remembering that they were but flesh, a wind that passeth away and cometh not again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.38-Ps.78.39">Ps. lxxviii. 38, 39</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen9386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9387" type="x-p"/> 1. The pious reflections Job makes upon his own life and death. Such plain truths as these concerning the shortness and vanity of life, the unavoidableness and irrecoverableness of death, <hi type="italic">then</hi> do us good when we think and speak of them with application to ourselves. Let us consider then, (1.) That we must shortly take our leave of all the things that are seen, that are temporal. The eye of the body must be closed, and shall no more see good, the good which most men set their hearts upon; for their cry is, <hi type="italic">Who will make us to see good?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Ps. iv. 6</reference>. If we be such fools as to place our happiness in visible good things, what will become of us when they shall be for ever hidden from our eyes, and we shall no more see good? Let us therefore live by that faith which is the substance and evidence of things not seen. (2.) That we must then remove to an invisible world: <hi type="italic">The eye of him that hath</hi> here <hi type="italic">seen me shall see me no more</hi> there. It is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hades</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">an unseen state,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.7.8">v. 8</reference>. Death removes our lovers and friends into darkness (<reference osisRef="Ps.88.18">Ps. lxxxviii. 18</reference>), and will shortly remove us out of their sight; when we <hi type="italic">go hence we shall be seen no more</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.13">Ps. xxxix. 13</reference>), but go to converse with the things that are not seen, that are eternal. (3.) That God can easily, and in a moment, put an end to our lives, and send us to another world (<reference osisRef="Job.7.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thy eyes are upon me and I am not;</hi> thou canst look me into eternity, frown me into the grave, when thou pleasest." <div eID="gen9387" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen9388"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9389"/>Shouldst thou, displeased, give me a frowning look,<l eID="gen9389" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9390"/>I sink, I die, as if with lightning struck. Sir <hi type="small-caps">R. Blackmore</hi> .<l eID="gen9390" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen9388"/> <div sID="gen9391" type="x-p"/> He takes away our breath, and we die; nay, he but <hi type="italic">looks on the earth</hi> and it <hi type="italic">trembles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.14.29-Ps.14.30">Ps. xiv. 29, 30</reference>. (4.) That, when we are once removed to another world, we must never return to this. There is constant passing from this world to the other, but <hi type="italic">vestigia nulla retrorsum—there is no repassing.</hi> "Therefore, Lord, kindly ease me by death, for that will be a perpetual ease. I shall return no more to the calamities of this life." When we are dead we are gone, to return no more, [1.] From our house under ground (<reference osisRef="Job.7.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more</hi> until the general resurrection, shall come up no more to his place in this world. Dying is work that is to be done but once, and therefore it had need be well done: an error there is past retrieve. This is illustrated by the blotting out and scattering of a cloud. It is consumed and vanisheth away, is resolved into air and never knits again. Other clouds arise, but the same cloud never returns: so a new generation of the children of men is raised up, but the former generation is quite consumed and vanishes away. When we see a cloud which looks great, as if it would eclipse the sun and drawn the earth, of a sudden dispersed and disappearing, let us say, "Just such a thing is the life of man; it is <hi type="italic">a vapour that appears for a little while and then vanishes away.</hi>" [2.] To return no more to our house above ground (<reference osisRef="Job.7.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall return no more to his house,</hi> to the possession and enjoyment of it, to the business and delights of it. Others will take possession, and keep it till they also resign to another generation. The rich man in hell desired that Lazarus might be sent to his house, knowing it was to no purpose to ask that he might have leave to go himself. Glorified saints shall return no more to the cares, and burdens, and sorrows of their house; nor damned sinners to the gaieties and pleasures of their house. Their place shall no more know them, no more own them, have no more acquaintance with them, nor be any more under their influence. It concerns us to secure a better place when we die, for this will no more own us. <div eID="gen9391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9392" type="x-p"/> 2. The passionate inference he draws from it. From these premises he might have drawn a better conclusion that this (<reference osisRef="Job.7.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak; I will complain.</hi> Holy David, when he had been meditating on the frailty of human life, made a contrary use of it (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.3">Ps. xxxix. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">I was dumb, and opened not my mouth</hi>); but Job, finding himself near expiring, hastens as much to make his complaint as if he had been to make his last will and testament or as if he could not die in peace until he had given vent to his passion. When we have but a few breaths to draw we should spend them in the holy gracious breathings of faith and prayer, not in the noisome noxious breathings of sin and corruption. Better die praying and praising than die complaining and quarrelling. <div eID="gen9392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9393" type="x-p"/> II. As a distempered man, sorely and grievously distempered both in body and mind. In this part of his representation is he is very peevish, as if God dealt hardly with him and laid upon him more than was meet: "<hi type="italic">Am I a sea, or a whale</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.7.12">v. 12</reference>), a raging sea, that must be kept within bounds, to check its proud waves, or an unruly whale, that must be restrained by force from devouring all the fishes of the sea? Am I so strong that there needs so much ado to hold me? so boisterous that no less than all these mighty bonds of affliction will serve to tame me and keep me within compass?" We are very apt, when we are in affliction, to complain of God and his providence, as if he laid more restraints upon us that there is occasion for; whereas we are never in heaviness but when there is need, nor more than the necessity demands. 1. He complains that he could not rest in his bed, <reference osisRef="Job.7.13-Job.7.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. There we promise ourselves some repose, when we are fatigued with labour, pain, or traveling: "<hi type="italic">My bed shall comfort me, and my couch shall ease my complaint.</hi> Sleep will for a time give me some relief;" it usually does so; it is appointed for that end; many a time it has eased us, and we have awaked refreshed, and with new vigour. When it is so we have great reason to be thankful; but it was not so with poor Job: his bed, instead of comforting him, terrified him; and his couch, instead of easing his complaint, added to it; for if he dropped asleep, he was disturbed with frightful dreams, and when those awaked him still he was haunted with dreadful apparitions. This was it that made the night so unwelcome and wearisome to him as it was (<reference osisRef="Job.7.4">v. 4</reference>): When <hi type="italic">shall I arise?</hi> Note, God can, when he pleases, meet us with terror even where we promise ourselves ease and repose; nay, he can make us a terror to ourselves, and, as we have often contracted guilt by the rovings of an unsanctified fancy, he can likewise, by the power of our own imagination, create us much grief, and so make that our punishment which has often been our sin. In Job's dreams, though they might partly arise from his distemper (in fevers, or small pox, when the body is all over sore, it is common for the sleep to be unquiet), yet we have reason to think Satan had a hand, for he delights to terrify those whom it is out of his reach to destroy; but Job looked up to God, who permitted Satan to do this (<hi type="italic">thou scarest me</hi>), and mistook Satan's representations for the <hi type="italic">terror of God setting themselves in array against him.</hi> We have reason to pray to God that our dreams may neither defile nor disquiet us, neither tempt us to sin nor torment us with fear, that he who keeps Israel, and neither slumbers nor sleeps, may keep us when we slumber and sleep, that the devil may not then do us a mischief, either as an insinuating serpent or as a roaring lion, and to bless God if we lie down and our sleep is sweet and we are not thus scared. 2. He covets to rest in his grave, that bed where there are no tossings to and fro, nor any frightful dreams, <reference osisRef="Job.7.15-Job.7.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. (1.) He was sick of life, and hated the thoughts of it: "<hi type="italic">I loathe it;</hi> I have had enough of it. <hi type="italic">I would not live always,</hi> not only not live always in this condition, in pain and misery, but not live always in the most easy and prosperous condition, to be continually in danger of being thus reduced. <hi type="italic">My days are vanity</hi> at the best, empty of solid comfort, exposed to real griefs; and I would not be for ever tied to such uncertainty." Note, A good man would not (if he might) live always in this world, no, not though it smile upon him, because it is a world of sin and temptation and he has a better world in prospect. (2.) He was fond of death, and pleased himself with the thoughts of it: his <hi type="italic">soul</hi> (his judgment, he thought, but really it was his passion) <hi type="italic">chose strangling and death rather than life;</hi> any death rather than such a life as this. Doubtless this was Job's infirmity; for though a good man would not wish to live always in this world, and would choose strangling and death rather than sin, as the martyrs did, yet he will be content to live as long as pleases God, not choose death rather than life, because life is our opportunity of glorifying God and getting ready for heaven.
entries.069e59ed923b37e6f56c07b2b9f8433bf89d4b95: <div eID="gen9393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9394" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> What <hi type="italic">is</hi> man, that thou shouldest magnify him? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? 18 And <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou shouldest visit him every morning, <hi type="italic">and</hi> try him every moment? <hi type="super">19</hi> How long wilt thou not depart from me, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle? 20 I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men? why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to myself? <hi type="super">21</hi> And why dost thou not pardon my transgression, and take away mine iniquity? for now shall I sleep in the dust; and thou shalt seek me in the morning, but I <hi type="italic">shall</hi> not <hi type="italic">be.</hi> <div eID="gen9394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9395" type="x-p"/> Job here reasons with God, <div eID="gen9395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9396" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning his dealings with man in general (<reference osisRef="Job.7.17-Job.7.18">v. 17, 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">What is man, that thou shouldst magnify him?</hi> This may be looked upon either, 1. As a passionate reflection upon the proceedings of divine justice; as if the great God did diminish and disparage himself in contending with man. "Great men think it below them to take cognizance of those who are much their inferiors so far as to reprove and correct their follies and indecencies; why then does God magnify man, by visiting him, and trying him, and making so much ado about him? Why will he thus pour all his forces upon one that is such an unequal match for him? Why will he visit him with afflictions, which, like a quotidian ague, return as duly and constantly as the morning light, and try, every moment, what he can bear?" We mistake God, and the nature of his providence, if we think it any lessening to him to take notice of the meanest of his creatures. Or, 2. As a pious admiration of the condescensions of divine grace, like that, <reference osisRef="Ps.8.4">Ps. viii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.3">cxliv. 3</reference>. He owns God's favour to man in general, even when he complains of his own particular troubles. "<hi type="italic">What is man,</hi> miserable man, a poor, mean, weak creature, <hi type="italic">that thou,</hi> the great and glorious God, shouldst deal with him as thou dost? What is man," (1.) "That thou shouldst put such honour upon him, <hi type="italic">shouldst magnify him,</hi> by taking him into covenant and communion with thyself?" (2.) "That thou shouldst concern thyself so much about him, <hi type="italic">shouldst set thy heart upon him,</hi> as dear to thee, and one that thou hast a kindness for?" (3.) "<hi type="italic">That thou shouldst visit him</hi> with thy compassions <hi type="italic">every morning,</hi> as we daily visit a particular friend, or as the physician visits his patients every morning to help them?" (4.) "That thou shouldst <hi type="italic">try him,</hi> shouldst feel his pulse and observe his looks, <hi type="italic">every moment,</hi> as in care about him and jealous over him?" That such a worm of the earth as man is should be the darling and favourite of heaven is what we have reason for ever to admire. <div eID="gen9396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9397" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning his dealings with him in particular. Observe, <div eID="gen9397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9398" type="x-p"/> 1. The complaint he makes of his afflictions, which he here aggravates, and (as we are all too apt to do) makes the worst of, in three expressions:—(1.) That he was the butt to God's arrows: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast set me as a mark against thee,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.7.20">v. 20</reference>. "My case is singular, and none is shot at as I am." (2.) That he was a <hi type="italic">burden to himself,</hi> ready to sink under the load of his own life. How much delight soever we take in ourselves God can, when he pleases, make us burdens to ourselves. What comfort can we take in ourselves if God appear against us as an enemy and we have not comfort in him. (3.) That he had no intermission of his griefs (<reference osisRef="Job.7.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">How long</hi> will it be ere thou cause thy rod to <hi type="italic">depart from me,</hi> or abate the rigour of the correction, at least for so long as that I may <hi type="italic">swallow down my spittle?</hi>" It should seem, Job's distemper lay much in his throat, and almost choked him, so that he could not swallow his spittle. He complains (<reference osisRef="Job.30.18">ch. xxx. 18</reference>) that it <hi type="italic">bound him about like the collar of his coat.</hi> "Lord," says he, "wilt not thou give me some respite, some breathing time?" <reference osisRef="Job.9.18">ch. ix. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen9398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9399" type="x-p"/> 2. The concern he is in about his sins. The best men have sin to complain of, and the better they are the more they will complain of it. (1.) He ingenuously owns himself guilty before God: <hi type="italic">I have sinned.</hi> God had said of him that he was a <hi type="italic">perfect and an upright man;</hi> yet he says of himself, <hi type="italic">I have sinned.</hi> Those may be upright who yet are not sinless; and those who are sincerely penitent are accepted, through a Mediator, as evangelically perfect. Job maintained, against his friends, that he was not a hypocrite, not a wicked man; and yet he owned to his God that he had sinned. If we have been kept from gross acts of sin, it does not therefore follow that we are innocent. The best must acknowledge, before God, that they have sinned. His calling God the <hi type="italic">observer,</hi> or <hi type="italic">preserver,</hi> of men, may be looked upon as designed for an aggravation of his sin: "Though God has had his eye upon me, his eye upon me for good, yet I have sinned against him." When we are in affliction it is seasonable to confess sin, as the procuring cause of our affliction. Penitent confessions would drown and silence passionate complaints. (2.) He seriously enquires how he may make his peace with God: "<hi type="italic">What shall I do unto thee,</hi> having done so much against thee?" Are we convinced that we have sinned, and are we brought to own it? We cannot but conclude that something must be done to prevent the fatal consequences of it. The matter must not rest as it is, but some course must be taken to undo what has been ill done. And, if we are truly sensible of the danger we have run ourselves into, we shall be willing to do any thing, to take a pardon upon any terms; and therefore shall be <hi type="italic">inquisitive as to what we shall do</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.7">Mic. vi. 6, 7</reference>), what we shall do to God, not to satisfy the demands of his justice (that is done only by the Mediator), but to qualify ourselves for the tokens of his favour, according to the tenour of the gospel-covenant. In making this enquiry it is good to eye God as the preserver or Saviour of men, not their destroyer. In our repentance we must keep up good thoughts of God, as one that delights not in the ruin of his creatures, but would rather they should return and live. "Thou art the Saviour of men; be my Saviour, for I cast myself upon thy mercy." (3.) He earnestly begs for the forgiveness of his sins, <reference osisRef="Job.7.21">v. 21</reference>. The heat of his spirit, as, on the one hand, it made his complaints the more bitter, so, on the other hand, it made his prayers the more lively and importunate; as here: <hi type="italic">"Why dost thou not pardon my transgression?</hi> Art thou not a God of infinite mercy, that art ready to forgive? Hast not thou wrought repentance in me? Why then dost thou not give me the pardon of my sin, and make me to hear the voice of that joy and gladness?" Surely he means more than barely the removing of his outward trouble, and is herein earnest for the return of God's favour, which he complained of the want of, <reference osisRef="Job.6.4">ch. vi. 4</reference>. "Lord, pardon my sins, and give me the comfort of that pardon, and then I can easily bear my afflictions," <reference osisRef="Matt.9.2">Matt. ix. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Isa. xxxiii. 24</reference>. When the mercy of God pardons the transgression that is committed by us the grace of God takes away the iniquity that reigns in us. Wherever God removes the guilt of sin he breaks the power of sin. (4.) To enforce his prayer for pardon he pleads the prospect he had of dying quickly: <hi type="italic">For now shall I sleep in the dust.</hi> Death will lay us in the dust, will lay us to sleep there, and perhaps presently, now in a little time. Job had been complaining of restless nights, and that sleep departed from his eyes (<reference osisRef="Job.7.3-Job.7.4">v. 3, 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.7.13">13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.7.14">14</reference>); but those who cannot sleep on a bed of down will shortly sleep in a bed of dust, and not be scared with dreams nor tossed to and fro: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt seek me in the morning,</hi> to show me favour, but <hi type="italic">I shall not be;</hi> it will be too late then. If my sins be not pardoned while I live, I am lost and undone for ever." Note, The consideration of this, that we must shortly die, and perhaps may die suddenly, should make us all very solicitous to get our sins pardoned and our iniquity taken away.  <chapter eID="Job.7"/> <div eID="gen9399" type="x-p"/>

entries.65ffc7a25bd247178f69d1c99c859e7c6bbb6193: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4583"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.7.1-Job.7.21">Job 7:1-21</reference>. Job Excuses His Desire for Death.</title> <div sID="gen6638" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4583"/><hi type="bold">1. appointed time--</hi>better, "a warfare," hard conflict with evil (so in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Is 40:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.1">Da 10:1</reference>). Translate it "appointed time" (<reference osisRef="Job.14.14">Job 14:14</reference>). Job reverts to the sad picture of man, however great, which he had drawn (<reference osisRef="Job.3.14">Job 3:14</reference>), and details in this chapter the miseries which his friends will see, if, according to his request (<reference osisRef="Job.6.28">Job 6:28</reference>), they will look on him. Even the Christian soldier, "warring a good warfare," rejoices when it is completed (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.3">2Ti 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8">8</reference>). <div eID="gen6638" type="x-p"/>
entries.eeb24cd880db71707276bba45cd004fc85259363: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4584"/><div sID="gen6639" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4584"/><hi type="bold">2. earnestly desireth--</hi>Hebrew, "pants for the [evening] shadow." Easterners measure time by the length of their shadow. If the servant longs for the evening when his wages are paid, why may not Job long for the close of his hard service, when he shall enter on his "reward?" This proves that Job did not, as many maintain, regard the grave as a mere sleep.<div eID="gen6639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.--</hi>Months of comfortless misfortune.<div eID="gen6640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am made to possess--</hi>literally, "to be heir to." Irony. "To be heir to," is usually a matter of joy; but here it is the entail of an involuntary and dismal inheritance.<div eID="gen6641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Months--</hi>for days, to express its long duration.<div eID="gen6642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Appointed--</hi>literally, "they have numbered to me"; marking well the unavoidable doom assigned to him. <div eID="gen6643" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f5d248a7e7561bcb3f151f9cbd9edbe33d3e19e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4585"/><div sID="gen6644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4585"/>4. Literally, "When shall be the flight of the night?" [Gesenius]. Umbreit, not so well, "The night is long extended"; literally, "measured out" (so Margin). <div eID="gen6644" type="x-p"/>
entries.313d9044e32f2d5a656d0ad418e82ee54db8bd88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4586"/><div sID="gen6645" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4586"/>5. In elephantiasis maggots are bred in the sores (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.23">Ac 12:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">Is 14:11</reference>).<div eID="gen6645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clods of dust--</hi>rather, a crust of dried filth and accumulated corruption (<reference osisRef="Job.2.7">Job 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen6646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my skin is broken and ... loathsome--</hi>rather, comes together so as to heal up, and again breaks out with running matter [Gesenius]. More simply the Hebrew is, "My skin rests (for a time) and (again) melts away" (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.7">Psa 58:7</reference>). <div eID="gen6647" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5c880c37f582b0d33759550b6f20ad4886bf57d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4587"/><div sID="gen6648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4587"/>6. (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.12">Is 38:12</reference>). Every day like the weaver's shuttle leaves a thread behind; and each shall wear, as he weaves. But Job's thought is that his days must swiftly be cut off as a web;<div eID="gen6648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6649" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without hope--</hi>namely, of a recovery and renewal of life (<reference osisRef="Job.14.19">Job 14:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.15">1Ch 29:15</reference>). <div eID="gen6649" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fcb5c9f6966226e5d2a192de3e5c31cea55af6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4588"/><div sID="gen6650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4588"/>7. Address to God.<div eID="gen6650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Wind--</hi>a picture of evanescence (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.39">Psa 78:39</reference>).<div eID="gen6651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall no more see--</hi>rather, "shall no more return to see good." This change from the different wish in <reference osisRef="Job.3.17">Job 3:17</reference>, &c., is most true to nature. He is now in a softer mood; a beam from former days of prosperity falling upon memory and the thought of the unseen world, where one is seen no more (<reference osisRef="Job.7.8">Job 7:8</reference>), drew from him an expression of regret at leaving this world of light (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.7">Ec 11:7</reference>); so Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.11">Is 38:11</reference>). Grace rises above nature (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.8">2Co 5:8</reference>). <div eID="gen6652" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ee8a18407e7310f3cab18a74720016dc63117af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4589"/><div sID="gen6653" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4589"/>8. The eye of him who beholds me (present, not past), that is, in the very act of beholding me, seeth me no more.<div eID="gen6653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6654" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thine eyes are upon me, and I am not--</hi>He disappears, even while God is looking upon him. Job cannot survive the gaze of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.32">Psa 104:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.11">Re 20:11</reference>). Not, "Thine eyes seek me and I am not to be found"; for God's eye penetrates even to the unseen world (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.8">Psa 139:8</reference>). Umbreit unnaturally takes "thine" to refer to one of the three friends. <div eID="gen6654" type="x-p"/>
entries.f81c91f0a1601bab302da28b8b363f39ce0fbdc1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4590"/><div sID="gen6655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4590"/>9. (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.23">2Sa 12:23</reference>).<div eID="gen6655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the grave--</hi>the Sheol, or place of departed spirits, not disproving Job's belief in the resurrection. It merely means, "He shall come up no more" in the present order of things. <div eID="gen6656" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e0f790d4979e231e5312f7623a6d7c8270795f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4591"/><div sID="gen6657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4591"/>10. (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.16">Psa 103:16</reference>). The Oriental keenly loves his dwelling. In Arabian elegies the desertion of abodes by their occupants is often a theme of sorrow. Grace overcomes this also (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.29">Lu 18:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.34">Ac 4:34</reference>). <div eID="gen6657" type="x-p"/>
entries.2edf1574557daa17782f3733bbffe37fa64fa118: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4592"/><div sID="gen6658" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4592"/>11. Therefore, as such is my hard lot, I will at least have the melancholy satisfaction of venting my sorrow in words. The Hebrew opening words, "Therefore I, at all events," express self-elevation [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6658" type="x-p"/>
entries.cacd05b97e370869e4ce31c8f4f189bad43f718c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4593"/><div sID="gen6659" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4593"/>12. Why dost thou deny me the comfort of care-assuaging sleep? Why scarest thou me with frightful dreams?<div eID="gen6659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Am I a sea--</hi>regarded in Old Testament poetry as a violent rebel against God, the Lord of nature, who therefore curbs his violence (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.22">Jr 5:22</reference>).<div eID="gen6660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or a whale--</hi>or some other sea monster (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Is 27:1</reference>), that Thou needest thus to watch and curb me? The Egyptians watched the crocodile most carefully to prevent its doing mischief. <div eID="gen6661" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed9bfd5883f230a59c44d44e1d182421fb7b9e48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4594"/><div sID="gen6662" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4594"/>14. The frightful dreams resulting from elephantiasis he attributes to God; the common belief assigned all night visions to God. <div eID="gen6662" type="x-p"/>
entries.acb7dcff841b34bd42ac4bd9a118393be6be11b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4595"/><div sID="gen6663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4595"/><hi type="bold">15. Umbreit translates, "So that I could wish to strangle myself--</hi>dead by my own hands." He softens this idea of Job's harboring the thought of suicide, by representing it as entertained only in agonizing dreams, and immediately repudiated with horror in <reference osisRef="Job.7.16">Job 7:16</reference>, "Yet that (self-strangling) I loathe." This is forcible and graphic. Perhaps the meaning is simply, "My soul chooses (even) strangling (or any violent death) rather than my life," literally, "my bones" (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.10">Psa 35:10</reference>); that is, rather than the wasted and diseased skeleton, left to him. In this view, "I loathe it" (<reference osisRef="Job.7.16">Job 7:16</reference>) refers to his life. <div eID="gen6663" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f542e24ab36fc74961800b1a7740c2855232787: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4596"/><div sID="gen6664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4596"/><hi type="bold">16. Let me alone--</hi>that is, cease to afflict me for the few and vain days still left to me. <div eID="gen6664" type="x-p"/>
entries.419fc99de137f9a296435484313701863f2fb144: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4597"/><div sID="gen6665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4597"/>17. (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.4">Psa 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.3">144:3</reference>). Job means, "What is man that thou shouldst make him [of so much importance], and that thou shouldst expend such attention [or, heart-thought] upon him" as to make him the subject of so severe trials? Job ought rather to have reasoned from God's condescending so far to notice man as to try him, that there must be a wise and loving purpose in trial. David uses the same words, in their right application, to express wonder that God should do so much as He does for insignificant man. Christians who know God manifest in the man Christ Jesus may use them still more. <div eID="gen6665" type="x-p"/>
entries.87944132bf49c7a96f9c76da51953749994bf28f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4598"/><div sID="gen6666" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4598"/>18. With each new day (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.14">Psa 73:14</reference>). It is rather God's mercies, not our trials, that are new every morning (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.23">La 3:23</reference>). The idea is that of a shepherd taking count of his flock every morning, to see if all are there [Cocceius]. <div eID="gen6666" type="x-p"/>
entries.d16c61c1feab93d6b77e18f72fa45470d2765471: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4599"/><div sID="gen6667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4599"/>19. How long (like a jealous keeper) wilt thou never take thine eyes off (so the Hebrew for "depart from") me? Nor let me alone for a brief respite (literally, "so long as I take to swallow my spittle"), an Arabic proverb, like our, "till I draw my breath." <div eID="gen6667" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a4b1f5a9e61eafe87bd6b5e48daf79c50da4341: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4600"/><div sID="gen6668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4600"/><hi type="bold">20. I have sinned--</hi>Yet what sin can I do against ("to," <reference osisRef="Job.35.6">Job 35:6</reference>) thee (of such a nature that thou shouldst jealously watch and deprive me of all strength, as if thou didst fear me)? Yet thou art one who hast men ever in view, ever watchest them--O thou Watcher (<reference osisRef="Job.7.12">Job 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.14">Da 9:14</reference>) of men. Job had borne with patience his trials, as sent by God (<reference osisRef="Job.1.21">Job 1:21</reference>; 2:10); only his reason cannot reconcile the ceaseless continuance of his mental and bodily pains with his ideas of the divine nature.<div eID="gen6668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set me as a mark--</hi>Wherefore dost thou make me thy point of attack? that is, ever assail me with new pains? [Umbreit] (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.12">La 3:12</reference>). <div eID="gen6669" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a26b789be9d8d1a80683c44ca6a489cbdb90f89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4601"/><div sID="gen6670" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4601"/><hi type="bold">21. for now--</hi>very soon.<div eID="gen6670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the morning--</hi>not the resurrection; for then Job will be found. It is a figure, from one seeking a sick man in the morning, and finding he has died in the night. So Job implies that, if God does not help him at once, it will be too late, for he will be gone. The reason why God does not give an immediate sense of pardon to awakened sinners is that they think they have a claim on God for it. <chapter eID="Job.7"/>

entries.911c1b04db6f8d51d07e9648f82ab999f3195273: <div eID="gen16147" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16148" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16149" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16149" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16148" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16150" type="x-p"/> Job continues to deplore his helpless and afflicted state, <reference osisRef="Job.7.1-Job.7.6">Job 7:1-6</reference>. He expostulates with God concerning his afflictions, <reference osisRef="Job.7.7-Job.7.12">Job 7:7-12</reference>; describes the disturbed state of his mind by visions in the night season; abhors life, <reference osisRef="Job.7.13-Job.7.16">Job 7:13-16</reference>; and, showing that he is unworthy of the notice of God, begs pardon and respite, <reference osisRef="Job.7.17-Job.7.21">Job 7:17-21</reference>. <div eID="gen16150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16151" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen16151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16152" type="x-p"/> Is there not an appointed time to man - The Hebrew, with its literal rendering, is as follows: הלא צבא לאנוש עלי ארץ halo tsaba leenosh aley arets, "Is there not a warfare to miserable man upon the earth?" And thus most of the versions have understood the words. The Septuagint: Ποτερον ουχι πειρατηριον εστι ὁ βιος ανθρωπου επι της γης; "Is not the life of man a place of trial upon earth?" The Vulgate: Militia est vita hominis super terram, "The life of man is a warfare upon earth?" The Chaldee is the same. N'y a-t-il pas comme un train de guerre ordonne aux mortels sur la terre? "Is there not a continual campaign ordained for mortals upon the earth?" French Bible. The German and Dutch the same. Coverdale: Is not the life off man upon earth a very batayle? Carmarden, Rouen, 1566: Hath man any certayne tyme upon earth? Syriac and Arabic: "Now, man has time upon the earth." Non e egli il tempo determinato a l'huomo sopra la terra?" "Is there not a determined time to man upon the earth?" Bib. Ital., 1562. All these are nearer to the true sense than ours; and of a bad translation, worse use has been made by many theologians. I believe the simple sentiment which the writer wished to convey is this: Human life is a state of probation; and every day and place is a time and place of exercise, to train us up for eternal life. Here is the exercise, and here the warfare: we are enlisted in the bands of the Church militant, and must accomplish our time of service, and be honorably dismissed from the warfare, having conquered through the blood of the Lamb; and then receive the reward of the heavenly inheritance.
entries.ade2d1ea2c1813777909a38d28a5f53fc7fcc2d9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16153" type="x-p"/> Earnestly desireth the shadow - As a man who labors hard in the heat of the day earnestly desires to get under a shade, or wishes for the long evening shadows, that he may rest from his labor, get his day's wages, retire to his food, and then go to rest. Night is probably what is meant by the shadow; as in Virgil, Aen. iv., ver. 7: <div eID="gen16153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16154" type="x-p"/> Humentemque Aurora polo dimoverat Umbram. "The morning had removed the humid shadow, i.e., night, from the world." <div eID="gen16154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16155" type="x-p"/> Where Servius justly observes: <div eID="gen16155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16156" type="x-p"/> Nihil interest, utrum Umbram an Noctem dicat: Nox enim Umbra terrae est, "It makes no difference whether he says shadow or night; for night is the shadow of the earth."
entries.4a358780f28d078f7288510d4773f52a5a4f9b79: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16157" type="x-p"/> So am I made to possess - But night is no relief to me, it is only a continuance of my anxiety and labor. I am like the hireling, I have my appointed labor for the day. I am like the soldier harassed by the enemy: I am obliged to be continually on the watch, always on the look out, with scarcely any rest.
entries.063b0408bf44c375bfb6ceb8441a1545c58f5441: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16158" type="x-p"/> When I lie down - I have so little rest, that when I do lie down I long for the return of the light, that I may rise. Nothing can better depict the state of a man under continual afflictions, which afford him no respite, his days and his nights being spent in constant anguish, utterly unable to be in any one posture, so that he is continually changing his position in his bed, finding ease nowhere: thus, as himself expresses it, he is full of tossings.
entries.73886005119d728dd308f07440348ce8dc5fe62b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16159" type="x-p"/> My flesh is clothed with worms - This is perhaps no figure, but is literally true: the miserably ulcerated state of his body, exposed to the open air, and in a state of great destitution, was favorable to those insects that sought such places in which to deposit their ova, which might have produced the animals in question. But the figure is too horrid to be farther illustrated. <div eID="gen16159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16160" type="x-p"/> Clods of dust - I believe all the commentators have here missed the sense. I suppose Job to allude to those incrustations of indurated or dried pus, which are formed on the tops of pustules in a state of decay: such as the scales which fall from the pustules of the smallpox, when the patient becomes convalescent. Or, if Job's disease was the elephantiasis, it may refer to the furfuraceous scales which are continually falling off the body in that disorder. It is well known, that in this disease the skin becomes very rigid, so as to crack across, especially at the different joints, out of which fissures a loathsome ichor is continually exuding. To something like this the words may refer, My Skin is Broken, and become Loathsome.
entries.add378e2abd98d78870c7cf9d7621200ad704cb8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16161" type="x-p"/> Swifter than a weaver's shuttle - The word ארג areg signifies rather the weaver than his shuttle. And it has been doubted whether any such instrument were in use in the days of Job. Dr. Russell, in his account of Aleppo, shows that though they wove many kinds of curious cloth, yet no shuttle was used, as they conducted every thread of the woof by their fingers. That some such instrument as the shuttle was in use from time immemorial, there can be no doubt: and it is certain that such an instrument must have been in the view of Job, without which the figure would lose its expression and force. In almost every nation the whole of human existence has been compared to a web; and the principle of life, through the continual succession of moments, hours, days, weeks, months, and years, to a thread woven through that web. Hence arose the fable of the Parcae or Fates, called also the Destinies or Fatal Sisters. They were the daughters of Erebus and Nox, darkness and night; and were three in number, and named Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos. Clotho held the distaff; Lachesis spun off the thread; and Atropos cut it off with her scissors, when it was determined that life should end. Job represents the thread of his life as being spun out with great rapidity and tenuity, and about to be cut off. <div eID="gen16161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16162" type="x-p"/> And are spent without hope - Expectation of future good was at an end; hope of the alleviation of his miseries no longer existed. The hope of future good is the balm of life: where that is not, there is despair; where despair is, there is hell. The fable above mentioned is referred to by Virgil, Ecl. iv., ver. 46, but is there applied to time: - <div eID="gen16162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16163" type="x-p"/> Talia Secla, suis dixerunt, currite, fusis <div eID="gen16163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16164" type="x-p"/> Concordes stabili fatorum numine Parcae. "The Fates, when they this happy thread have spun <div eID="gen16164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16165" type="x-p"/> Shall bless the sacred clue, and bid it smoothly run." <div eID="gen16165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16166" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen16166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16167" type="x-p"/> Isaiah uses the same figure, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.12">Isa 38:12</reference> : - <div eID="gen16167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16168" type="x-p"/> My life is cut off, as by the weaver: <div eID="gen16168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16169" type="x-p"/> He will sever me from the loom. <div eID="gen16169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16170" type="x-p"/> In the course of the day thou wilt finish my web. <div eID="gen16170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16171" type="x-p"/> Lowth. <div eID="gen16171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16172" type="x-p"/> Coverdale translates thus: My dayes passe over more spedely then a weaver can weave out his webbe and are gone or I am awarre. <div eID="gen16172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16173" type="x-p"/> A fine example of this figure is found in the Teemour Nameh, which I shall give in Mr. Good's translation: - "Praise be to God, who hath woven the web of human affairs in the loom of his will and of his wisdom, and hath made waves of times and of seasons to flow from the fountain of his providence into the ocean of his power." The simile is fine, and elegantly expressed.
entries.692499daa9ad74c7d873925352cf91ffa7972045: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16174" type="x-p"/> My life is wind - Mr. Good translates, "O remember that, if my life pass away, mine eye shall turn no more to scenes of goodness;" which he paraphrases thus: "O remember that, if my life pass away, never more shall I witness those scenes of Divine favor, never more adore thee for those proofs of unmerited mercy, which till now have been so perpetually bestowed on me." I think the common translation gives a very good sense.
entries.7d4f9707ca5ff13184e44d4571160d53a870c16a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16175" type="x-p"/> Shall see me no more - If I die in my present state, with all this load of undeserved odium which is cast upon me by my friends, I shall never have an opportunity of vindicating my character, and regaining the good opinion of mankind. <div eID="gen16175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16176" type="x-p"/> Thine eyes are upon one, and I am not - Thou canst look me into nothing. Or, Let thine eye be upon me as judged to death, and I shall immediately cease to live among men.
entries.02f21b2b29b90d216b031803f64fd5f9abec0b6d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16177" type="x-p"/> As the cloud is consumed - As the cloud is dissipated, so is the breath of those that go down to the grave. As that cloud shall never return, so shall it be with the dead; they return no more to sojourn with the living. See on the following verses.
entries.d02f0b3a615af32ea6c12dfb4080d2778d738caf: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16178" type="x-p"/> He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more - He does not mean that he shall be annihilated but that he shall never more become an inhabitant of the earth. The word שאול, which we properly enough translate grave, here signifies also the state of the dead, hades, and sometimes any deep pit, or even hell itself.
entries.82240d50db1b483e2e43dc3d635ba0bd020bff28: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16179" type="x-p"/> Therefore I will not refrain - All is hopeless; I will therefore indulge myself in complaining.
entries.d3fc97afb4ac4a6464aad5191c231b36af96fd03: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16180" type="x-p"/> Am I a sea, or a whale - "Am I condemned as the Egyptians were who were drowned in the Red Sea? or am I as Pharaoh, who was drowned in it in his sins, that thou settest a keeper over me?" Targum. Am I as dangerous as the sea, that I should be encompassed about with barriers, lest I should hurt mankind? Am I like an ungovernable wild beast or dragon, that I must be put under locks and bars? I think our own version less exceptionable than any other hitherto given of this verse. The meaning is sufficiently plain. Job was hedged about and shut in with insuperable difficulties of various kinds; he was entangled as a wild beast in a net; the more he struggled, the more he lost his strength, and the less probability there was of his being extricated from his present situation. The sea is shut in with barriers, over which it cannot pass; for God has "placed the sand for the bound of the sea by a perpetual decree, that it cannot pass it: and though the waves thereof toss themselves, yet can they not prevail; though they roar, yet can they not pass over it," <reference osisRef="Jer.5.22">Jer 5:22</reference>. "For thou hast set a bound that they may not pass over; that they turn not again to cover the earth;" <reference osisRef="Psa.104.9">Psa 104:9</reference>. "Or who shut up the sea with doors, when it brake forth, as if it had issued out of the womb? When I made the cloud the garment thereof, and thick darkness a swaddling band for it, and brake up for it my decreed place, and set bars and doors; and said, Hitherto shalt thou come, but no farther: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed;" <reference osisRef="Job.38.8">Job 38:8</reference>. Here then is Job's allusion: the bounds, doors, garment, swaddling bands, decreed place, and bars, are the watchers or keepers which God has set to prevent the sea from overflowing the earth; so Job's afflictions and distresses were the bounds and bars which God had apparently set to prevent him from injuring his fellow creatures. At least Job, in his complaint, so takes it. Am I like the sea, which thou hast imprisoned within bounds, ready to overwhelm and destroy the country? or am I like a dragon, which must be cooped up in the same way, that it may not have the power to kill and destroy? Surely in my prosperity I gave no evidence of such a disposition; therefore should not be treated as a man dangerous to society. In this Job shows that he will not refrain his mouth.
entries.deaf6689f4c27203d29390f078ef804afbd17e40: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16181" type="x-p"/> Thou sparest me with dreams - There is no doubt that Satan was permitted to haunt his imagination with dreadful dreams and terrific appearances; so that, as soon as he fell asleep, he was suddenly roused and alarmed by those appalling images. He needed rest by sleep, but was afraid to close his eyes because of the horrid images which were presented to his imagination. Could there be a state more deplorable than this?
entries.5629c43d4712a036457c5c8e7bdbd56d6c390910: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16182" type="x-p"/> Chooseth strangling - It is very likely that he felt, in those interrupted and dismal slumbers, an oppression and difficulty of breathing something like the incubus or nightmare; and, distressing as this was, he would prefer death by this means to any longer life in such miseries.
entries.2f7bf498b1c998b54ca8a7138c9f6a2987265bc7: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16183" type="x-p"/> I loathe it; I would not live alway - Life, in such circumstances, is hateful to me; and though I wish for long life, yet if length of days were offered to me with the sufferings which I now undergo, I would despise the offer and spurn the boon. Mr. Good is not satisfied with our common version, and has adopted the following, which in his notes he endeavors to illustrate and defend: <reference osisRef="Job.7.15">Job 7:15</reference> So that my soul coveteth suffocation,And death in comparison with my suffering. <reference osisRef="Job.7.16">Job 7:16</reference> No longer would I live! O, release me!How are my days vanity!
entries.2165bc3e2de0d90d4266e3dbc28fec76fe72a511: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16184" type="x-p"/> What is man that thou shouldest magnify him? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? - Two different ideas have been drawn from these words: - <div eID="gen16184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16185" type="x-p"/> 1. Man is not worth thy notice; why therefore dost thou contend with him? <div eID="gen16185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16186" type="x-p"/> 2. How astonishing is thy kindness that thou shouldest fix thy heart - thy strongest affections, on such a poor, base, vile, impotent creature as man, (אנוש enosh), that thou shouldest so highly exalt him beyond all other creatures, and mark him with the most particular notice of thy providence and grace! <div eID="gen16186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16187" type="x-p"/> The paraphrase of Calmet is as follows: "Does man, such as he at present is, merit thy attention! What is man that God should make it his business to examine, try, prove, and afflict him? Is it not doing him too much honor to think thus seriously about him? O Lord! I am not worthy that thou shouldest concern thyself about me!"
entries.3ec98f0e736830ac68893777b499e2aa77a4aaa2: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16188" type="x-p"/> Till I swallow down my spittle? - This is a proverbial expression, and exists among the Arabs to the present day; the very language being nearly the same. It signifies the same as, Let me draw my breath; give me a moment's space; let me have even the twinkling of an eye. I am urged by my sufferings to continue my complaint; but my strength is exhausted, my mouth dry with speaking. Suspend my sufferings even for so short a space as is necessary to swallow my spittle, that my parched tongue may be moistened, so that I may renew my complaint.
entries.fd94b596d5e1a4660aa810d7d118c143d4227dc2: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16189" type="x-p"/> I have sinned; what shall I do - Dr. Kennicott contends that these words are spoken to Eliphaz, and not to God, and would paraphrase them thus: "You say I must have been a sinner. What then? I have not sinned against thee, O thou spy upon mankind! Why hast thou set up me as a butt or mark to shoot at? Why am I become a burden unto thee? Why not rather overlook my transgression, and pass by mine iniquity? I am now sinking to the dust! To-morrow, perhaps, I shall be sought in vain!" See his vindication of Job at the end of these notes on this book. Others consider the address as made to God. Taken in this light, the sense is plain enough. Those who suppose that the address is made to God, translate the <reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference> thus: "Be it that I have sinned, what injury can I do unto thee, O thou Observer of man? Why hast thou set me up as a mark for thee, and why am I made a burden to thee?" The Septuagint is thus: Ει εγω ἡμαρτον, τι δυνησομαι πραξαι, ὁ επισταμενος τον νουν των ανθρωπων; If I have sinned, what can I do, O thou who knowest the mind of men? Thou knowest that it is impossible for me to make any restitution. I cannot blot out my offenses; but whether I have sinned so as to bring all these calamities upon me, thou knowest, who searchest the hearts of men.
entries.93db8ebcd1fa16f82da1f57eaf0121663b5d9f5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16190" type="x-p"/> And why dost thou not pardon - These words are spoken after the manner of men. If thou have any design to save me, if I have sinned, why dost thou not pardon my transgression, as thou seest that I am a dying man; and to-morrow morning thou mayest seek me to do me good, but in all probability I shall then be no more, and all thy kind thoughts towards me shall be unavailing? If I have sinned, then why should not I have a part in that mercy that flows so freely to all mankind? That Job does not criminate himself here, as our text intimates, is evident enough from his own repeated assertions of his innocence. And it is most certain that Bildad, who immediately answers, did not consider him as criminating but as justifying himself; and this is the very ground on which he takes up the subject. Were we to admit the contrary, we should find strange inconsistencies, if not contradictions, in Job's speeches: on such a ground the controversy must have immediately terminated, as he would then have acknowledged that of which his friends accused him; and here the book of Job would have ended.  <chapter eID="Job.7"/> <div eID="gen16190" type="x-p"/>

entries.39450e7e17e86e3828961357e5f59fc379535066: <reference osisRef="Job.7.1-Job.3.1">Job 7:1-3   1</reference>  Has not a man warfare upon earth, <div eID="gen7095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7096" type="x-p"/> And his days are like the days of a hireling?   2  Like a servant who longs for the shade, <div eID="gen7096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7097" type="x-p"/> And like a hireling who waits for his wages,   3  So am I made to possess months of disappointment, <div eID="gen7097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7098" type="x-p"/> And nights of weariness are appointed to me. <div eID="gen7098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7099" type="x-p"/> The conclusion is intended to be: thus I wait for death as refreshing and rest after hard labour. He goes, however, beyond this next point of comparison, or rather he remains on this side of it. צבא is not service of a labourer in the field, but active military service, then fatigue, toil in general (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.20">Isa 40:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.1">Dan 10:1</reference>). <reference osisRef="Job.7.2">Job 7:2</reference> Ewald and others translate incorrectly: as a slave longs, etc. כּ can never introduce a comparative clause, except an infinitive, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference>, which can then under the regimen of this כּ be continued by a <hi type="italic">verb. fin.;</hi> but it never stands directly for כּאשׁר, as כּמו does in rare instances. In <reference osisRef="Isa.5.3">Isa 5:3</reference>, שׁוא retains its primary signification, nothingness, error, disappointment (<reference osisRef="Job.15.31">Job 15:31</reference>): months that one after another disappoint the hope of the sick. By this it seems we ought to imagine the friends as not having come at the very commencement of his disease. Elephantiasis is a disease which often lasts for years, and slowly but inevitably destroys the body. On מנּוּ, <hi type="italic">adnumeraverunt</hi> = <hi type="italic">adnumeratae sunt</hi>, vid., Ges. §137, 3*.
entries.09459aab7dd6b3a8bd1e73f6d14dcda53ba98b3b: <reference osisRef="Job.7.4-Job.6.4">Job 7:4-6   4</reference>  If I lie down, I think: <div eID="gen7099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7100" type="x-p"/> When shall I arise and the evening break away? <div eID="gen7100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7101" type="x-p"/> And I become weary with tossing to and fro unto the morning dawn.   5  My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of earth; <div eID="gen7101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7102" type="x-p"/> My skin heals up to fester again.   6  My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle, <div eID="gen7102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7103" type="x-p"/> And vanish without hope. <div eID="gen7103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7104" type="x-p"/> Most modern commentators take מדּד as <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> from מדד: the night is extended (Renan: <hi type="italic">la nuit se prolonge</hi>), which is possible; comp. Ges. §52, 2. But the metre suggests another rendering: מדּד constr. of מדּד from נדד, to flee away: and when fleeing away of the evening. The night is described by its commencement, the late evening, to make the long interval of the sleeplessness and restlessness of the invalid prominent. In נדדים and מדד there is a play of words (Ebrard). רמּה, worms, in reference to the putrifying ulcers; and גּוּשׁ (with זעירא )ג, clod of earth, from the cracked, scaly, earth-coloured skin of one suffering with elephantiasis. The <hi type="italic">praett</hi>. are used of that which is past and still always present, the <hi type="italic">futt. consec.</hi> of that which follows in and with the other. The skin heals, רגע (which we render with Ges., Ew., <hi type="italic">contrahere se</hi>); the result is that it becomes moist again. ימּאס, according to Ges. §67, rem. 4 = ימּס, Psa 58:8. His days pass swiftly away; the result is that they come to an end without any hope whatever. ארג is like κερκίς, <hi type="italic">radius</hi>, a weaver’s shuttle, by means of which the weft is shot between the threads of the warp as they are drawn up and down. His days pass as swiftly by as the little shuttle passes backwards and forwards in the warp. <div eID="gen7104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7105" type="x-p"/> Next follows a prayer to God for the termination of his pain, since there is no second life after the present, and consequently also the possibility of requital ceases with death.
entries.19f5657a0bb7afe4727b8b7154732395c22aec90: Job 7:7-11   7  Remember that my life is a breath, <div eID="gen7105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7106" type="x-p"/> That my eye will never again look on prosperity.   8  The eye that looketh upon me seeth me no more; <div eID="gen7106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7107" type="x-p"/> Thine eyes look for me, - I am no more!   9  The clouds are vanished and passed away, <div eID="gen7107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7108" type="x-p"/> So he that goeth down to Sheôl cometh not up. 10  He returneth no more to his house, <div eID="gen7108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7109" type="x-p"/> And his place knoweth him no more. 11  Therefore I will not curb my mouth; <div eID="gen7109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7110" type="x-p"/> I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; <div eID="gen7110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7111" type="x-p"/> I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. <div eID="gen7111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7112" type="x-p"/> We see good, i.e., prosperity and joy, only in the present life. It ends with death. שׁוּב with ל <hi type="italic">infin</hi>. is a synonym of הוסיף, Job 20:9. No eye (עין <hi type="italic">femin</hi>.) which now sees me (prop. eye of my seer, as <reference osisRef="Gen.16.13">Gen 16:13</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.20.7">Job 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.12">Psa 31:12</reference>, for ראני, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">Isa 29:15</reference>, or ראני, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">Isa 47:10</reference>; according to another reading, ראי: no eye of seeing, i.e., no eye with the power of seeing, from ראי, vision) sees me again, even if thy eyes should be directed towards me to help me; my life is gone, so that I can no more be the subject of help. For from Sheôl there is no return, no resurrection (comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.103.16">Psa 103:16</reference> for the expression); therefore will I at least give free course to my thoughts and feelings (comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4">Psa 77:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.38.15">Isa 38:15</reference>, for the expression). The גּם, <reference osisRef="Job.7.11">Job 7:11</reference>, is the so-called גם <hi type="italic">talionis;</hi> the parallels cited by Michalis are to the point, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.43">Eze 16:43</reference>; Mal 2:9; Psa 52:7. Here we first meet with the name of the lower world; and in the book of Job we learn the ancient Israelitish conception of it more exactly than anywhere else. We have here only to do with the name in connection with the grammatical exposition. שׁאול (usually <hi type="italic">gen. fem.</hi>) is now almost universally derived from שׁאל = שׁעל, to be hollow, to be deepened; and aptly so, for they imagined the <hi type="italic">Sheôl</hi> as under ground, as Num 16:30, Num 16:33 alone shows, on which account even here, as from <reference osisRef="Gen.37.35">Gen 37:35</reference> onwards, שׁאולה ירד is everywhere used. It is, however, open to question whether this derivation is correct: at least passages like <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab 2:5</reference>; Pro 30:15., show that in the later usage of the language, שׁאל, to demand, was thought of in connection with it; derived from which <hi type="italic">Sheôl</hi> signifies (1) the appointed inevitable and inexorable demanding of everything earthly (an infinitive noun like אלוהּ, פּקוד); (2) conceived of as space, the place of shadowy duration whither everything on earth is demanded; (3) conceived of according to its nature, the divinely appointed fury which gathers in and engulfs everything on the earth. Job knows nothing of a demanding back, a redemption from <hi type="italic">Sheôl</hi>.
entries.14aa945c3b6e1e78815e78d29fed4ca7c0f77c4c: Job 7:12-16 12  Am I a sea or a sea-monster, <div eID="gen7112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7113" type="x-p"/> That thou settest a watch over me? 13  For I said, My bed shall comfort me; <div eID="gen7113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7114" type="x-p"/> My couch shall help me to bear my complaint. 14  Then thou scaredst me with dreams, <div eID="gen7114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7115" type="x-p"/> And thou didst wake me up in terror from visions, 15  So that my soul chose suffocation, <div eID="gen7115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7116" type="x-p"/> Death rather than this skeleton. 16  I loathe it, I would not live alway; <div eID="gen7116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7117" type="x-p"/> Let me alone, for my days are breath. <div eID="gen7117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7118" type="x-p"/> Since a watch on the sea can only be designed to effect the necessary precautions at its coming forth from the shores, it is probable that the poet had the Nile in mind when he used ים, and consequently the crocodile by תּנּין. The Nile is also called ים in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.5">Isa 19:5</reference>, and in Homer ὠκεανός, Egyptian <hi type="italic">oham</hi> (= ὠκεανός), and is even now called (at least by the Bedouins) <hi type="italic">bahhr</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">bahr</hi>). The illustrations of the book, says von Gerlach correctly, are chiefly Egyptian. On the contrary, Hahn thinks the illustration is unsuitable of the Nile, because it is not watched on account of its danger, but its utility; and Schlottman thinks it even small and contemptible without assigning a reason. The figure is, however, appropriate.
