As watches are set to keep the Nile in channels as soon as it breaks forth, and as men are set to watch that they may seize the crocodile immediately he moves here or there; so Job says all his movements are checked at the very commencement, and as soon as he desires to be more cheerful he feels the pang of some fresh pain. In <reference osisRef="Job.7.13">Job 7:13</reference>, ב after נשׂא is partitive, as Num 11:17; Mercier correctly: <hi type="italic">non nihil querelam meam levabit.</hi> If he hopes for such repose, it forthwith comes to nought, since he starts up affrighted from his slumber. Hideous dreams often disturb the sleep of those suffering with elephantiasis, says Avicenna (in Stickel, S. 170). Then he desires death; he wishes that his difficulty of breathing would increase to suffocation, the usual end of elephantiasis. מחנק is absolute (without being obliged to point it מחנק with Schlottm.), as e.g., מרמס, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa 10:6</reference> (Ewald, §160, <hi type="italic">c</hi>). He prefers death to these his bones, i.e., this miserable skeleton or framework of bone to which he is wasted away. He despises, i.e., his life, Job 9:21. Amid such suffering he would not live for ever. הבל, like רוּח, Job 7:7.
entries.3ce88e5079a5c5d83f98ff974ffdc9153ffeae17: Job 7:17-19 17  What is man that Thou magnifiest him, <div eID="gen7118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7119" type="x-p"/> And that Thou turnest Thy heart toward him, 18  And visitest him every morning, <div eID="gen7119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7120" type="x-p"/> Triest him every moment? 19  How long dost Thou not look away from me, <div eID="gen7120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7121" type="x-p"/> Nor lettest me alone till I swallow down my spittle? <div eID="gen7121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7122" type="x-p"/> The questions in Job 7:17. are in some degree a parody on <reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.144.3">Psa 144:3</reference>, Lam 3:23. There it is said that God exalts puny man to a kingly and divine position among His creatures, and distinguishes him continually with new tokens of His favour; here, that instead of ignoring him, He makes too much of him, by selecting him, perishable as he is, as the object of ever new and ceaseless sufferings. כּמּה, <hi type="italic">quamdiu</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.7.19">Job 7:19</reference>, is construed with the <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. instead of the <hi type="italic">fut.:</hi> how long will it continue that Thou turnest not away Thy look of anger from me? as the synonymous עד־מתי, <hi type="italic">quousque</hi>, is sometimes construed with the <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. instead of the <hi type="italic">fut.,</hi> e.g., Psa 80:5. “Until I swallow my spittle” is a proverbial expression for the minimum of time.
entries.2f08dc553b5656754ebc32b5789589b1e1958497: Job 7:20-21 20  Have I sinned - what could I do to Thee?! <div eID="gen7122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7123" type="x-p"/> O Observer of men, <div eID="gen7123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7124" type="x-p"/> Why dost Thou make me a mark to Thee, <div eID="gen7124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7125" type="x-p"/> And am I become a burden to Thee? 21  And why dost Thou not forgive my transgression, <div eID="gen7125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7126" type="x-p"/> And put away my iniquity? <div eID="gen7126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7127" type="x-p"/> For now I will lay myself in the dust, <div eID="gen7127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7128" type="x-p"/> And Thou seekest for me, and I am no more.  “I have sinned” is hypothetical (Ges. §155, 4, <hi type="italic">a</hi>): granted that I have sinned. According to Ewald and Olsh., אפעל־לך מה defines it more particularly: I have sinned by what I have done to Thee, in my behaviour towards Thee; but how tame and meaningless such an addition would be! It is an inferential question: what could I do to Thee? i.e., what harm, or also, since the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. may be regulated by the <hi type="italic">praet.:</hi> what injury have I thereby done to Thee? The thought that human sin, however, can detract nothing from the blessedness and glory of God, underlies this. With a measure of sinful bitterness, Job calls God האדם נצר, the strict and constant observer of men, <hi type="italic">per convicium fere,</hi> as Gesenius not untruly observes, nevertheless without a breach of <hi type="italic">decorum divinum</hi> (Renan: <hi type="italic">O Espion de l'homme</hi>), since the appellation, in itself worthy of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">Isa 27:3</reference>), is used here only somewhat unbecomingly. מפגּע is not the target for shooting at, which is rather מטּרה (<reference osisRef="Job.16.12">Job 16:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.12">Lam 3:12</reference>), but the object on which one rushes with hostile violence (בּ פּגע). Why, says Job, hast Thou made me the mark of hostile attack, and why am I become a burden to Thee? It is not so in our text; but according to Jewish tradition, עלי, which we now have, is only a סופרים תקון, <hi type="italic">correctio scribarum,</hi><note placement="foot">Vid., the <hi type="italic">Commentary on Habakkuk</hi>, S. 206-208; comp. Geiger, <hi type="italic">Urschrift und Uebersetzungen der Bibel</hi>, S. 308ff.</note> for אליך, which was removed as bordering on blasphemy: why am I become a burden to Thee, so that Thou shouldest seek to get rid of me? This reading I should not consider as the original, in spite of the tradition, if it were not confirmed by the lxx, εἰμὶ δὲ ἐπὶ σοὶ φορτίον. <div eID="gen7128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7129" type="x-p"/> It is not to be objected, that he who is fully conscious of sin cannot consider the strictest divine punishment even of the smallest sin unjust. The suffering of one whose habitual state is pleasing to God, and who is conscious of the divine favour, can never be explained from, and measured according to, his infirmities: the infirmities of one who trusts in God, or the believer, and the severity of the divine justice in the punishment of sin, have no connection with one another. Consequently, when Eliphaz bids Job regard his affliction as chastisement, Job is certainly in the wrong to dispute with God concerning the magnitude of it: he would rather patiently yield, if his faith could apprehend the salutary design of God in his affliction; but after his affliction once seems to him to spring from wrath and enmity, and not from the divine purpose of mercy, after the phantom of a hostile God is come between him and the brightness of the divine countenance, he cannot avoid falling into complaint of unmercifulness. For this the speech of Eliphaz is in itself not to blame: he had most feelingly described to him God’s merciful purpose in this chastisement, but he is to blame for not having taken the right tone. <div eID="gen7129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7130" type="x-p"/> The speech of Job is directed against the unsympathetic and reproving tone which the friends, after their long silence, have assumed immediately upon his first manifestation of anguish. He justifies to them his complaint (ch. 3) as the natural and just outburst of his intense suffering, desires speedy death as the highest joy with which God could reward his piety, complains of his disappointment in his friends, from whom he had expected affectionate solace, but by whom he sees he is now forsaken, and earnestly exhorts them to acknowledge the justice of his complaint (ch. 6). But can they? Yes, they might and should. For Job thinks he is no longer an object of divine favour: an inward conflict, which is still more terrible than hell, is added to his outward suffering. For the damned must give glory to God, because they recognise their suffering as just punishment: Job, however, in his suffering sees the wrath of God, and still is at the same time conscious of his innocence. The faith which, in the midst of his exhaustion of body and soul, still knows and feels God to be merciful, and can call him “my God,” like Asaph in Ps 73, - this faith is well-nigh overwhelmed in Job by the thought that God is his enemy, his pains the arrows of God. The assumption is false, but on this assumption Job’s complaints (ch. 3) are relatively just, including, what he himself says, that they are mistaken, thoughtless words of one in despair. But that despair is sin, and therefore also those curses and despairing inquiries! <div eID="gen7130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7131" type="x-p"/> Is not Eliphaz, therefore, in the right? His whole treatment is wrong. Instead of distinguishing between the complaint of his suffering and the complaint of God in Job’s outburst of anguish, he puts them together, without recognising the complaint of his suffering to be the natural and unblamable result of its extraordinary magnitude, and as a sympathizing friend falling in with it. But with regard to the complaints of God, Eliphaz, acting as though careful for his spiritual welfare, ought not to have met them with his reproofs, especially as the words of one heavily afflicted deserve indulgence and delicate treatment; but he should have combated their false assumption. First, he should have said to Job, “Thy complaints of thy suffering are just, for thy suffering is incomparably great.” In the next place, “Thy cursing thy birth, and thy complaint of God who has given thee thy life, might seem just if it were true that God has rejected thee; but that is not true: even in suffering He designs thy good; the greater the suffering, the greater the glory.” By this means Eliphaz should have calmed Job’s despondency, so as to destroy his false assumption; but he begins wrongly, and consequently what he says at last so truly and beautifully respecting the glorious issue of a patient endurance of chastisement, makes no impression on Job. He has not fanned the faintly burning wick, but his speech is a cold and violent breath which is calculated entirely to extinguish it. <div eID="gen7131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7132" type="x-p"/> After Job has defended the justice of his complaints against the insensibility of the friends, he gives way anew to lamentation. Starting from the wearisomeness of human life in general, he describes the greatness of his own suffering, which has received no such recognition on the part of the friends: it is a restless, torturing death without hope (<reference osisRef="Job.7.1-Job.7.6">Job 7:1-6</reference>). Then he turns to God: O remember that there is no second life after death, and that I am soon gone for ever; therefore I will utter my woe without restraint (<reference osisRef="Job.7.7-Job.7.11">Job 7:7-11</reference>). Thus far (from <reference osisRef="Job.6.1">Job 6:1</reference> onwards) I find in Job’s speech no trace of blasphemous or sinful despair. When he says (<reference osisRef="Job.6.8-Job.6.12">Job 6:8-12</reference>), How I would rejoice if God, whose word I have never disowned, would grant me my request, and end my life, for I can no longer bear my suffering, - I cannot with Ewald see in its despair rising to madness, which (<reference osisRef="Job.7.10">Job 7:10</reference>) even increases to frantic joy. For Job’s disease was indeed really in the eyes of men as hopeless as he describes it. In an incurable disease, however, imploring God to hasten death, and rejoicing at the thought of approaching dissolution, is not a sin, and is not to be called despair, inasmuch as one does not call giving up all hope of recovery despair. <div eID="gen7132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7133" type="x-p"/> Moreover, it must not be forgotten that the book of Job is an oriental book, and therefore some allowance must be made of the intensity and strength of conception of the oriental nature: then that it is a poetical book, and that frenzy and madness may not be also understood by the intensified expression in which poetry, which idealizes the real, clothes pain and joy: finally, that it is an Old Testament book, and that in the Old Testament the fundamental nature of man is indeed sanctified, but not yet subdued; the spirit shines forth as a light in a dark place, but the day, the ever constant consciousness of favour and life, has not yet dawned. The desire of a speedy termination of life (<reference osisRef="Job.6.8-Job.6.12">Job 6:8-12</reference>) is in <reference osisRef="Job.7.7-Job.7.11">Job 7:7-11</reference> softened down even to a request for an alleviation of suffering, founded on this, that death terminates life for ever. In the Talmud (<hi type="italic">b. Bathra,</hi> 16, <hi type="italic">a</hi>) it is observed, on this passage, that Job denies the resurrection of the dead (המתים בתחיים איוב שׁכפר מכאן); but Job knows nothing of a resurrection of the dead, and what one knows not, one cannot deny. He knows only that after death, the end of the present life, there is no second life in this world, only a being in <hi type="italic">Sheôl</hi>, which is only an apparent existence = no existence, in which all praise of God is silent, because He no longer reveals himself there as to the living in this world (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">Psa 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.30.10">Psa 30:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.11-Ps.88.13">Psa 88:11-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.115.17">Psa 115:17</reference>). From this chaotic conception of the other side of the grave, against which even the psalmists still struggle, the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead had not been set forth at the time of Job, and of the author of the book of Job. The restoration of Israel buried in exile (Ezek 37) first gave the impulse to it; and the resurrection of the Prince of Life, who was laid in the grave, set the seal upon it. The resurrection of Jesus Christ was first of all the actual overthrow of Hades.<hi type="italic">Mortis seu inferni, observes Brentius, in accordance with Scriptures, ea conditio est, ut natura sua quoscunque comprehenderit tantisper teneat nec dimittat, dum Christus, filius Dei, morte ad infernum descenderit, h.e. perierit; per hunc enim devicta morte et inferno liberantur quotquot fide renovati sunt.</hi> This great change in the destiny of the dead was incomplete, and the better hope which became brighter and brighter as the advent of death’s Conqueror drew near was not yet in existence. For if after death, or what is the same thing, after the descent into Sheôl, there was only a non-existence for Job, it is evident that on the one hand he can imagine a life after death only as a return to the present world (such a return does, however, not take place), on the other hand that no divine revelation said anything to him of a future life which should infinitely compensate for a return to the present world. And since he knows nothing of a future existence, it can consequently not be said that he denies it: he knows nothing of it, and even his dogmatizing friends have nothing to tell him about it. We shall see by and by, how the more his friends torment him, the more he is urged on in his longing for a future life; but the word of revelation, which could alone change desire into hope, is wanting. The more tragic and heart-rending Job’s desire to be freed by death from his unbearable suffering is, the more touching and importunate is his prayer that God may consider that now soon he can no longer be an object of His mercy. Just the same request is found frequently in the Psalms, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.89.48">Psa 89:48</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.103.14-Ps.103.16">Psa 103:14-16</reference> : it involves nothing that is opposed to the Old Testament fear of God. Thus far we can trace nothing of frenzy and madness, and of despair only in so far as Job has given up the hope (נואשׁ) of his restoration, - not however of real despair, in which a man impatiently and forcibly snaps asunder the bond of trust which unites him to God. If the poet had anywhere made Job to go to such a length in despair, he would have made Satan to triumph over him. <div eID="gen7133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7134" type="x-p"/> Now, however, the last two strophes follow in which Job is hurried forward to the use of sinful language, <reference osisRef="Job.7.12-Job.7.16">Job 7:12-16</reference> : Am I a sea or a sea-monster, etc.; and <reference osisRef="Job.7.17-Job.7.21">Job 7:17-21</reference> : What is man, that thou accountest him so great, etc. We should nevertheless be mistaken if we thought there were sin here in the expressions by which Job describes God’s hostility against himself. We may compare e.g., <reference osisRef="Lam.3.9">Lam 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.10">Lam 3:10</reference> : “He hath enclosed my ways with hewn stone, He hath made any paths crooked; He is to me as a bear lying in wait, a lion in the thicket.” It is, moreover, not Job’s peculiar sin that he thinks God has changed to an enemy against him; that is the view which comes from his vision being beclouded by the conflict through which he is passing, as is frequently the case in the Psalms. His sin does not even consist in the inquiries, How long? and Wherefore? The Psalms in that case would abound in sin. But the sin is that he dwells upon these doubting questions, and thus attributes apparent mercilessness and injustice to God. And the friends constantly urge him on still deeper in this sin, the more persistently they attribute his suffering to his own unrighteousness. Jeremiah (in Lamentations 3), after similar complaints, adds: Then I repeated this to my heart, and took courage from it: the mercies of Jehovah, they have no end; His compassions do not cease, etc. Many of the Psalms that begin sorrowfully, end in the same way; faith at length breaks through the clouds of doubt. But it should be remembered that the change of spiritual condition which, e.g., in <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.10">Psa 6:1-10</reference>, is condensed to the narrow limits of a lyric composition of eleven verses, is here in Job worked out with dramatical detail as a passage of his life’s history: his faith, once so heroic, only smoulders under ashes; the friends, instead of fanning it to a flame, bury it still deeper, until at last it is set free from its bondage by Jehovah himself, who appears in the whirlwind. Bildad’s First Speech - Job 8<note placement="foot">We will give an example here of our and Ewald’s computation of the strophes. “In the speech of Bildad, ch. 8,” says Ewald, <hi type="italic">Jahrb</hi>. ix. 35, “the first part may go to <reference osisRef="Job.8.10">Job 8:10</reference>, and be divided into three strophes of three lines each.” This is right; but that the three strophes consist of three lines, i.e., according to Ewald’s use of the word, three (<hi type="italic">Masoretic</hi>) verses, is accidental. There are three strophes, of which the first consists of six lines = stichs, the second of seven, the third again of six. “Just so them,” Ewald proceeds, “the second part, <reference osisRef="Job.8.11-Job.8.19">Job 8:11-19</reference>, is easily broken up into like three strophes,” viz., <reference osisRef="Job.8.11-Job.8.13">Job 8:11-13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.8.14-Job.8.16">Job 8:14-16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.8.17">Job 8:17</reference>-19. But strophes must first of all be known as being groups of stichs forming a complete sense (<hi type="italic">Sinngruppen</hi>). They are, according to their idea, groups of measured compass, as members of a symmetrical whole. Can we, however, take <reference osisRef="Job.8.14-Job.8.16">Job 8:14-16</reference> together as such a complete group? In his edition of Job of 1854, Ewald places a semicolon after <reference osisRef="Job.8.16">Job 8:16</reference>; and rightly, for <reference osisRef="Job.8.16-Job.8.19">Job 8:16-19</reference> belong inseparably together. Taking them thus, we have in the second part of the speech three groups. In the first, <reference osisRef="Job.8.11-Job.8.15">Job 8:11-15</reference>, the godless are likened to the reed; and his house in prosperity to a spider’s web, since its perishableness, symbolized by the reed, is proved (אשׁר, <reference osisRef="Job.8.14">Job 8:14</reference>). In the second, <reference osisRef="Job.8.16-Job.8.19">Job 8:16-19</reference>, follows the figure of the climbing plant which <reference osisRef="Job.8.19">Job 8:19</reference> (יצמחוּ) seems to indicate. In the third, <reference osisRef="Job.8.20-Job.8.22">Job 8:20-22</reference>, the figure is given up, and the strophe is entirely <hi type="italic">epimythionic</hi>. Of these three groups, the first consists of ten, the second of eight, and the third of six lines = stichs. The schema is therefore as we have given it above: 6. 7. 6. 10. 8. 6. We are only justified in calling these groups strophes by the predominance of the hexastich, which occurs at the beginning, middle, and close of the speech.</note>  <chapter eID="Job.7"/> <div eID="gen7134" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="4">4. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 28. 67. Chap. 17. 12.</ns0:note> When I lie down <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To get some rest and sleep.</ns0:note>, I say, when shall I arise, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the Evening be measured.</ns0:note> the night <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>the evening.</ns0:hi> The part put for the whole, as it is, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 1. 5.</ns0:note> be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">From side to side in the Bed, as men in grievous pains of body, or anxiety of mind use to be.</ns0:note> unto the dawning of the day <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">So this Hebrew word is used also, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 30. 17. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 119. 147.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. My flesh is clothed <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Covered all over as with a garment.</ns0:note> with worms <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which oft breed and break forth in divers parts of living bodies, as history and ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perience witnesseth, and which were easily bred out of <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rupted flesh and sores.</ns0:note>, and clods of dust <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either the dust of the earth upon which he lay, which his sores would quickly lick up; or the scabs of his sores, which by degrees mouldred away into dust.</ns0:note>; my skin is broken <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">By Ulcers breaking forth in all parts of it.</ns0:note>, and become loathsom.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:note> My daies are swifter <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The time of my life hastens to a period; And therefore vain are those hopes which you give me of a restitution to my former prosperity in this world.</ns0:note> than a Weavers Shuttle <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Which passeth in a moment from one end of the web to the other.</ns0:note>, and are spent without hope <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">To wit; of enjoying any good day here.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. O remember <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">He turneth his speech to God as appears from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8. 12. 14.</ns0:note> that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 89. 47.</ns0:note> my life is wind <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> vain, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 57. 13. <ns0:hi>Hose.</ns0:hi> 8 7. quickly passing away so as never to come again, as is said <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 78. 39.</ns0:note>; mine eye <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                        <ns0:hi>To see,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>to enjoy.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> see good <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Enjoy (for so <ns0:hi>seeing</ns0:hi> is sometimes used, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 34. 12. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 17. 6.) good, to wit, in this world, as my friends flatter me. Compare <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 14. 12. & 19. 26, 27.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. The eye of him that hath seen me shall see me no more: <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">In this mortall state: I shall never return to this life again.</ns0:note> thine eyes <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> upon me, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">That is, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> live no <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> I am not <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either, 1. If thou doest but cast one angry look upon me, <ns0:hi>I am not, i. e.</ns0:hi> I am a dead man. So that phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 5. 24. & 42. 13. & 44. 20. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 103. 16. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 31. 15. Or, 2. <ns0:hi>When thine Eyes</ns0:hi> shall be <ns0:hi>upon me, (i. e.</ns0:hi> when thou shalt look for me to do me good, thou wilt find that) <ns0:hi>I am not,</ns0:hi> that I am dead and gone, and uncapable of that bounty and goodness which thou givest to men in this world<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Comp. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 10. 15. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 50. 20.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> the Cloud is consumed <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Being dried up or dissolved by the heat of the Sun.</ns0:note> and vanisheth away <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Never returneth again.</ns0:note>; so <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Sam. 12<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> he that goeth down to <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> H<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> the grave shall come up no <ns0:hi>more</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To live a natural mortal life amongst men. For, that he doth not deny a future life is manifest from <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 19. 25, &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. He shall return no more to his house <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To enjoy his house and possessions again.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psa. 103. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> neither shall his place know him any more <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He shall no more be seen and known in his former habitation and condition by his friends and neighbours. The <ns0:hi>place</ns0:hi> put for the men of the place, as <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 8. 18. & 20. 9. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 37. 10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. Therefore <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Since my life is by the common condition of mankind so vain and short, and when once lost, without all hopes of recovery, and withal extremely miserable, I will plead with God for pity and relief before I die; knowing that I must now speak, or else for ever after hold my peace as to requests of this nature.</ns0:note> I will not refrain my mouth<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">I will not smother my bitter anguish within my own breast, which will make it intollerable, but I will give it vent, and ease my self by pouring forth complaints, and expostulating with my God, who, as I hope, will hear and help me one way or other.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. <ns0:hi>Am</ns0:hi> I a Sea, or a Whale <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Am I so great, and powerful, and dangerous a creature, that thou needest to use extraordinary power and violence to rule and subdue me? Am I as fierce and unruly as the Sea, which, if thou didst not set a watch over it, and bounds to it, would overwhelm the earth, and destroy mankind upon it? Or, am I a vast and ungovernable Sea-monster, which, if thou didst not restrain it by thy powerful providence, would overturn ships, and destroy men in it, and devour all the lesser fishes? Have I behaved my self to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards thee, or towards men, with such rage and violence, as to need such chains to be put upon me? Or, is my strength so great as that of the Sea, which can endure so many and long storms one after another, and yet can subsist under them, and after them? or, of a Whale, that can laugh at Darts and Spears? as is said <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 41. 29. No Lord, thou knowest that I am but a poor weak creature, which thou canst crush with the least touch of thy fin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger, without these violent and unsupportable pains and miseries; and that I have not been so fierce and boisterous in my carriage as to need or deserve these extraordinary calamities.</ns0:note>, that thou settest a watch over me <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">That thou shouldest guard and restrain me with such heavy and unexampled miseries, lest I should break into rebellion against thee, or into cruelty towards men.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 9. 27, 28.</ns0:note> When I say, my Bed shall comfort me, my Couch shall ease my complaint <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">By giving me sweet and quiet sleep, which may take off the sense of my torments for that while.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. Then thou scarest me with dreams <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">With sad and dreadful dreams arising either from that melan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />choly humour which is now so fixed in me and predominant over me, or from the Devils malice who by thy permission disturbs me in this manner; So that I am afraid to go to sleep, and my reme<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy proves as bad as my disease.</ns0:note>, and ter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rifiest me through visions <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The same thing with dreams: for there were not only day-visions, which were offered to mens sight, when they were awake; but also night-visions, which were presented to mens Fancy in their sleep and dreams. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 28. 12. & 41. 1, 2. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 2. 1, 31. & 4, 5, 10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:389" />15. So that my Soul chooseth <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Not simply and in it self, but comparatively, rather than such a wretched life.</ns0:note> strangling <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The most violent, so it be but a certain and sudden death.</ns0:note>, and death rather <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> than my <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> than my life <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>than my bones, i. e.</ns0:hi> than my body, for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />merly the Soul's dear and desired companion, or than to be in the body, which commonly consists of skin and flesh, and bones, but in <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> was in a manner nothing but a bundle of bones; for his skin was every where broken, and his flesh was quite consu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med; as he oft complains, and his bones also were not free from pain and torment: for as Satan's Commission reached to <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>bones, Iob</ns0:hi> 2. 5. so doubtless his Malice and wicked Design would engage him to execute it to the utmost.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 10. 1.</ns0:note> I loath <ns0:hi>it.</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">To wit, my life last mentioned.</ns0:note> I would not live alway: <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">In this World, if I might, no not in prosperity; for even such a life is but vanity, much less in this extremity of misery. Or, <ns0:hi>Let me not live for ever,</ns0:hi> lingring in this miserable manner, as if thou wouldest not suffer me to die, but hadst a design to perpetuate my torments. Or, <ns0:hi>let me not live out mine age,</ns0:hi> or the full time of my life, which by the course of nature, I might do; for so the Hebrew word <ns0:hi>Olam,</ns0:hi> is oft used: but cut me off, and that speedily.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 10. 20. & 14. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. Psal. 39. 13.</ns0:note> let me alone, <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Withdraw thy hand from me, either 1. thy supporting hand which preserves my life, and suffer me to die: Or rather 2. thy correcting hand, as this same phrase is used, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note> for my days are vanity <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either 1. my life is in it self, and in its best estate a most vain, unsatisfying, uncertain thing: do not add this evil to it to make it miserable. Or, 2. My life is a vain, decaying, and perishing thing, it will of it self quickly va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nish and depart, and doth not need to be forced from me by such exquisite torments.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 8. 4. & 144. 3. Heb. 26.</ns0:note> What <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> man that thou should'st magnifie him <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">What is there in that poor, mean, contemptible Creature called Man, <ns0:hi>miserable man,</ns0:hi> as this word signifies, which can in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duce or incline thee to take any notice of him, to shew him such respect, or to make such account of him? Man is not worthy of thy Favour, and he is below thy Anger. It is too great a con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />descention to thee, and too great an honour for man that thou wiltst contend with him, and draw forth all thy forces against him, as if he were a fit match for thee; whereas men use to neg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lect and slight mean Adversaries, and will not do them the honour to fight with them. Comp. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 24. 14. Therefore do not, O Lord, thus dishonour thy self, nor magnifie me. I acknowledge that even thy corrections are mercies and honours, but, Lord, let me be no more so honoured.</ns0:note>? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Have any regard to him so far as to afflict him, which though it be grievous in it self, espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially when it is aggravated as mine is, yet unto thy people it is a great mercy and blessing, as being highly necessary and useful to humble them, and purge them from sin, and prepare them for glory: as on the contrary, those wicked men whom thou doest despise and hate, and design to destroy, thou doest forbear to punish or afflict them.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. And <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> thou shouldest visit him <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">To wit, punish or chasten him, as the Word is oft used, as <ns0:hi>visiting</ns0:hi> is oft used, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20. 5. and 32. 34. and 34. 7.</ns0:note> every morning <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Every day. But he mentions the <ns0:hi>morning,</ns0:hi> either because that is the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ginning of the day, and so is put synecdochically for the whole day, as the <ns0:hi>evening,</ns0:hi> v. 4. is put for the whole night: Or he speaks of God after the manner of men, who rest and sleep in the night, but in the morning rise and go about their business, and visit or inspect those persons and things which they have a respect for, or care of.</ns0:note>, and try him <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Afflict him, which is oft called <ns0:hi>trying,</ns0:hi> because it doth indeed try a man's faith and patience, and perseverance. But this and the former Verse may possibly be otherwise under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood, not of afflictions, but of mercies. Having declared his loathing of life, and his passionate desire of death, and urged it with this consideration, that the <ns0:hi>days</ns0:hi> of his life were meer <ns0:hi>va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nity;</ns0:hi> he now pursues it with this expostulation, What is man, that vain, foolish Creature<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> that thou shouldst <ns0:hi>magnifie</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>regard,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>visit him,</ns0:hi> (to wit, with thy mercy and blessings, of which those words are commonly used, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> that thou shouldst so far ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nour and regard him, as by thy visitation to preserve his Spirit, or hold his Soul in life) and <ns0:hi>try him,</ns0:hi> which God doth not only by afflictions, but also by prosperity and outward blessings, which commonly detect a mans hypocrisie, and discover that corruption which before lay hid in his heart? Therefore, O Lord, do not thus magnifie, and visit me with thy mercy, but take away my life.</ns0:note> every moment?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19. How long wilt thou not depart from me <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">How long will it be ere thou withdraw thy afflicting hand from me? <ns0:hi>e i. e.</ns0:hi> for a little time; or that I may have a breathing time: A proverbial expression, like that <ns0:hi>Spanish</ns0:hi> Proverb, <ns0:hi>I <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> not time or liberty to spit out my spittle.</ns0:hi> Or this expression may have respect to <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s distempered and calamitous condition wherewith he was so overwhelmed, that he either had not strength, or could not take heed to spit out his spittle as he should have done, but swallowed it down, as sick and melancholy persons often do.</ns0:note>, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle <ns0:hi>e?</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20. I have sinned <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Although I am innocent and free from those cr<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ing sins, for which my friends suppose thou hast sent this uncommon judgment upon me, yet if thou beest strict to mark what is amiss, I freely confess that I am a sinner, and therefore obnoxious to thy justice, and I humbly beg thy pardon for it; as it follows, <ns0:hi>vers.</ns0:hi> 21. And therefore accept of this Confession.</ns0:note>, what shall I do unto thee <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">to satisfie thy Justice, or regain thy Favour. I can do nothing to purchase or deserve it, and therefore implore thy mercy to pardon my sins.</ns0:note>, O thou preserver of men <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">O thou who, as thou wast the Creator of man, delightest to be, and to be called the Preserver and Saviour of men; and that waitest to be kind and gracious to men from day to day, as occasion requires; do not deal with me in a way contrary to thy own Nature and Name, and to the manner of thy dealing with all the rest of Man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kind. Oth. <ns0:hi>O thou Observer of men;</ns0:hi> thou who dost exactly know and diligently observe all mens inward motions, and outward actions; and therefore if thou shalt be severe to mark mine ini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quities, as thou seemest to be, I have not what to say or do unto thee. Compare <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 9. 3, 15, 29. & 14. 4. Into which thou wiltst shoot all the Arrows of thy indignation.</ns0:note>? why <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 16. 12. Psal. 21. 12. Lam. 3. 12.</ns0:note> hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to my self <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e</ns0:hi> I am weary of my self, and of my life, being no way able to resist or endure the assaults of so potent an Adversary.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21. And why dost thou not pardon my transgres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion, and take away mine iniquity <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Seeing thou art so gracious to others, so ready to preserve and pardon them, why may not I hope for the same favour from thee?</ns0:note>? for now shall I sleep in the dust <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">If thou doest not speedily help me, it will be too late, I shall be dead, and so uncapable of those blessings which thou usest to give to men in the land of the living.</ns0:note>; and thou shalt seek me in the morn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, but I shall not be <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> When thou shalt diligently seek for me, that thou maiest shew favour to me, thou wilt find that I am dead and gone, and so wilt lose thy oppor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tunity: Help therefore speedily.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
